verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the holy ones who are [in Ephesus] and faithful in Christ Jesus:
verse.note: The brackets mark words that are missing from the earliest surviving copies of the letter, including the oldest papyrus and the original hands of the two major fourth-century codices. Most later manuscripts have them. Many scholars think the letter first circulated among several congregations in the region and that the place name was attached early; others hold that the words are original.

The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense here. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ,
just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, to be holy and blameless before him in love.
verse.note: The phrase can be read with what precedes (“holy and blameless before him in love”) or with what follows (“in love he predestined us”). The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, and translators and commentators are divided. The text takes it with what precedes.

verse.text: He predestined us for adoption as his own sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will,
verse.note: The Greek is the legal term for adoption, which in the Roman world typically meant taking a son in order to make him an heir. It is applied here to all believers, women as well as men; the point is the status of heir, picked up by “inheritance” in verse 14. Some translations render “adoption as his children.”

verse.text: to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he graced us in the Beloved.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our offenses, according to the riches of his grace,
verse.note: The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass” in current English mainly suggests entering property without permission, so “offense” is used instead. The meaning is not disputed; versions vary among “trespasses,” “transgressions” and “sins.”

verse.text: which he lavished on us with all wisdom and insight.
He made known to us the secret of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas the point here is that the plan has now been made known. Most versions keep “mystery” as an established technical term, so this rendering is an editorial choice against the majority tradition, though lexicons give “secret” as a primary gloss.

verse.text: as a plan for the fullness of the times: to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth—in him.
verse.note: The verb was used for summing up the points of a speech or argument, and Romans 13:9 uses it of the commandments being summed up in one saying. English versions vary: “gather together in one,” “unite,” “gather up.” “Sum up” keeps the ordinary sense; the idea is that everything finds its coherence and its point in Christ.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that this translation keeps where the reference is to God’s realm. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.”

verse.text: In him we were also made God’s inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will,
verse.note: The verb occurs only here in the New Testament and concerns assigning by lot or as an allotted share. It can mean “we were made God’s inheritance,” echoing the Old Testament picture of Israel as the Lord’s portion, or “we obtained an inheritance,” which is the more common English rendering, or simply “we were chosen.” The first suits the passive form and verse 18, but the question remains open.

verse.text: so that we who first hoped in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.

note.term: we who first hoped in Christ

verse.note: The verb means to hope beforehand. “We” may be Jewish believers, who hoped in the Messiah before the Gentile readers addressed as “you also” in verse 13, or it may be all believers, who hope in Christ ahead of the final fulfillment. The rendering allows both but leans toward the first.

verse.text: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the good news of your salvation, and believed, were sealed in him with the promised Holy Spirit,
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations already alternate between the two.

verse.text: who is the down payment on our inheritance until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.
verse.note: This was a commercial term for a first installment that secures a transaction and obliges the payer to pay the rest. “Guarantee” and “pledge” lose the point that the Spirit is itself the first part of what is to come. “Deposit” and “down payment” are used by several modern versions.

verse.text: For this reason I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the holy ones,
do not stop giving thanks for you as I remember you in my prayers,
asking that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,

note.term: a spirit of wisdom and revelation

verse.note: The Greek has no article and can mean a disposition given by God (“a spirit of wisdom”) or the Holy Spirit as the giver of wisdom and revelation (“the Spirit of wisdom”). Translations are divided. Many scholars favor a reference to God’s Spirit, since revelation is not a human quality.

verse.text: with the eyes of your heart enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the holy ones,
and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength,
which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly realms,
far above every rule and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
And he put all things in subjection under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the assembly,
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” is near-universal in English versions and readers know what it refers to; “assembly” is used here throughout so that one Greek word has one English word.

verse.text: which is his body, the fullness of the one who fills all things in every way.

note.term: the fullness of the one who fills all things in every way
note.traditional: the fullness of him who fills all in all

verse.note: The participle can be read as “who fills” or as “who is being filled,” and “fullness” can mean what fills something or what is filled. Most translations take it as here: the assembly is filled by Christ, who himself fills all things. Minority readings are that the assembly completes Christ, or that Christ is being filled by God.

verse.text: And you were dead in your offenses and sins,
verse.note: The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass” now chiefly suggests entering property without permission, so “offense” is used; the meaning itself is not disputed. It stands here beside the more general word “sins” with little difference in sense.

verse.text: in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the domain of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.
verse.note: The Greek has the time-word “age” followed by the ordinary word for “world,” an unusual pairing. Most translations smooth it to “the course of this world” or “the ways of this world.” The literal form is kept here because it reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come (compare verse 7). A minority of scholars have taken “Age” as the name of a personal power, but this is not widely accepted.

note.term: the ruler of the domain of the air, the spirit
note.traditional: the prince of the power of the air, the spirit

verse.note: The word usually rendered “power” or “authority” here most likely means the sphere over which authority is exercised, hence “domain.” The air was commonly thought of as the region where hostile spirits lived. In Greek “the spirit” is in the genitive case, so it may mean the ruler himself, or it may be a second thing he rules (“ruler of the domain of the air, of the spirit now at work”). The translation follows the more common reading.

verse.text: Among them we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, carrying out the wishes of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, just like the rest.
But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead in our offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
so that in the coming ages he might display the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift—
verse.note: The Greek pronoun is neuter, while “grace” and “faith” are both feminine nouns. Most scholars therefore take “this” to refer to the whole event of being saved by grace through faith. An old and still-held reading takes faith in particular to be what is called God’s gift.

verse.text: not from works, so that no one may boast.
For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance so that we would walk in them.
Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh—called “the uncircumcision” by what is called “the circumcision,” made in the flesh by hands—
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. It is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere in the New Testament.

verse.text: remember that at that time you were apart from Christ, excluded from citizenship in Israel and foreigners to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verse.note: The word can mean either a body of citizens (a state or “commonwealth”) or the status and rights of a citizen. Many translations choose “commonwealth.” “Citizenship” is used here because verse 19 answers this verse with the related word “fellow citizens.” Either way, the point is that Gentiles stood outside the people to whom God’s promises belonged.

verse.text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, the hostility, in his flesh,

note.term: the dividing wall of the barrier

verse.note: Many interpreters see an allusion to the stone balustrade in the Jerusalem temple, which carried inscriptions warning non-Jews not to pass it on pain of death. Others take the wall as an image for the Law of Moses, which was sometimes described as a fence around Israel. The two are not mutually exclusive, and the reference is uncertain.

note.traditional: having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments

verse.note: The Greek syntax across verses 14 and 15 can be construed in more than one way. “The hostility” may explain the dividing wall that was broken down, as here, or it may be the object of the following verb, alongside the law (“nullifying in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments”). “In his flesh,” which refers to Christ’s death, can likewise go with either verb. The translation keeps the Greek word order so that both readings remain possible.

verse.text: nullifying the law of commandments set out in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into one new person, making peace,
verse.note: The verb means to deprive something of force or effect, not to destroy it. Most translations have “abolished” or “set aside.” “Nullify” is used throughout this translation where the validity of a law or promise is at stake; the same verb appears in Romans 3:31, where Paul denies that faith nullifies the law. Scholars debate whether the law as a whole is meant here or the law in its role of dividing Jew from Gentile.

verse.text: and might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, having put the hostility to death by it.
And he came and proclaimed the good news of peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near;

note.term: proclaimed the good news of peace

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for announcing good news and is related to the noun traditionally rendered “gospel.” The verse echoes Isaiah 57:19 (“peace, peace to the far and to the near”) and Isaiah 52:7 (the messenger who announces peace). In Isaiah the “far” are probably Jews in exile; here they are the Gentiles.

verse.text: for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
So then, you are no longer foreigners and resident aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household,
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Some interpreters think it refers here specifically to Jewish believers, or to angels, but most take it as God’s people as a whole.

verse.text: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone,
verse.note: The word comes from Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek version, where it describes a stone laid in a foundation. That is the majority understanding here, where the image is of a building rising from its foundation. Some scholars argue instead for the capstone or keystone that completes a structure at the top.

verse.text: in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy sanctuary in the Lord,
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. “Sanctuary” is used for the latter throughout this translation to keep the distinction; most versions have “a holy temple” here. The image is of the community as the place where God lives, as verse 22 makes explicit.

verse.text: in whom you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verse.note: The sentence breaks off here without a verb. Paul digresses in verses 2–13 to explain his commission, then takes up the thought again in verse 14 with the same words, “For this reason.” Some translations supply a verb such as “am” or “pray” in verse 1; this one leaves the break visible, as the Greek does.

The Greek word is the ordinary plural for “nations” or “peoples.” In Jewish usage it meant the non-Jewish peoples, and that is its sense throughout this chapter. Elsewhere in this translation the same word appears as “nations” when peoples as such are meant.

verse.text: if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you:
by revelation the secret was made known to me, as I have already written briefly,
verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. “Mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul’s point is that the secret has been told and can be stated plainly, as verse 6 does.

verse.text: and in reading it you can perceive my insight into the secret of Christ,
which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit:
that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an everyday word for the announcement of good news, including public proclamations. The related verb in verse 8 is rendered with the same phrase.

verse.text: of which I became a servant according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to me according to the working of his power—
to me, less than the least of all the holy ones, this grace was given—to bring the Gentiles the good news of the unfathomable riches of Christ,
verse.note: Many translations have “saints”; others use “God’s people.” The word refers to all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense.

verse.text: and to enlighten everyone about the plan of the secret hidden for ages in God, who created all things,

note.traditional: fellowship (KJV, following a different Greek reading); administration; plan

verse.note: This is the same Greek word rendered “stewardship” in verse 2. It covers both the management entrusted to a steward and the arrangement by which something is managed. In verse 2 Paul’s own commission is in view; here most interpreters take it as God’s arrangement for carrying out the secret. Some translations use “administration” in both places.

verse.text: so that now, through the assembly, the many-sided wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly places,
verse.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” wherever the Greek word occurs.

verse.text: according to the purpose of the ages that he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord,
in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

note.traditional: by the faith of him; through faith in him

verse.note: The Greek is literally “through the faith of him.” The majority reading takes this as the believer’s faith in Christ. A substantial minority of scholars read it as Christ’s own faithfulness: “through his faithfulness.” The grammar allows either.

verse.text: So I ask you not to lose heart over my afflictions on your behalf, which are your glory.

note.term: I ask you not to lose heart
note.traditional: I desire that ye faint not

verse.note: The Greek states neither whom Paul is asking nor who might lose heart. Most translations take it as a request to the readers not to be discouraged by his imprisonment. It could also be a prayer to God, either that the readers not lose heart or, less probably, that Paul himself not lose heart.

Older versions have “tribulations” here; modern ones often have “sufferings.” The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship that presses on a person. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does.

verse.text: For this reason I bend my knees before the Father,
from whom every family in the heavens and on earth takes its name,
verse.note: The Greek word for “family” here means a clan or lineage descended from one father, and it is formed from the word for “father.” A Greek hearer therefore caught a link between “Father” and “family” that English cannot reproduce. The older rendering “the whole family” is grammatically less likely. “In the heavens” keeps the Greek plural.

verse.text: that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, so that you, rooted and grounded in love,
verse.note: “In love” stands between two clauses in the Greek and can attach to either. Most translations, like this one, take it with what follows. The edition of the Greek text translated here punctuates it with what precedes: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, in love.” The original manuscripts had no punctuation, so the question is one of interpretation.

verse.text: may have the strength to comprehend, with all the holy ones, what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled to all the fullness of God.
Now to him who is able to do beyond everything, far more than we ask or imagine, according to the power at work in us,
to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
So I, the prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you were called,
verse.note: “Walk” is a Semitic idiom for how a person conducts their life, familiar from the Septuagint. Many modern translations paraphrase it as “live.” It is kept here because the image recurs through the letter (see verse 17).

verse.text: with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
verse.note: “Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the mainstream modern rendering.

verse.text: making every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were also called in the one hope of your calling;
one Lord, one faith, one baptism;
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
Therefore it says: “When he ascended on high, he led captives into captivity; he gave gifts to people.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 68:18 (67:19 in the Septuagint), a psalm about God ascending in triumph. Both the Hebrew text and the Septuagint say that he “received gifts among people,” where Ephesians has “gave gifts to people.” A later Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave,” so the author may be following an existing line of interpretation, but how the wording arose is debated.

verse.text: Now what does “he ascended” mean, except that he also descended to the lower parts of the earth?

note.term: the lower parts of the earth
note.traditional: the lower parts of the earth

verse.note: The Greek can mean the regions beneath the earth, that is, the realm of the dead, or “the lower parts, namely the earth,” in which case the descent is Christ’s coming to earth. Early interpreters mostly took the first view; many modern scholars take the second, and a minority think of the Spirit’s descent after the ascension. The rendering leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.
And it was he who gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as shepherds and teachers,
verse.note: “Pastor” is the Latin word for shepherd and has since become the title of a church office. The Greek is the ordinary word for someone who tends a flock, used here as a picture of those who care for the community. “Shepherds and teachers” share a single article in Greek, which may indicate one group with two functions or two closely linked groups; this is disputed.

verse.text: to equip the holy ones for the work of service, for building up the body of Christ,
verse.note: The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

This was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, from waiting at table to delivering a commission. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession, which the Greek word did not. Most English translations use “ministry” here.

note.term: to equip the holy ones for the work of service
note.traditional: for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry

verse.note: Older translations took the three phrases of this verse as parallel, so that the leaders named in verse 11 themselves do the work of service. Most modern translations and scholars read it as here: the leaders equip the holy ones, and the holy ones do the work. The change of preposition in the Greek after the first phrase favors this, but the older reading still has defenders.

verse.text: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full-grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,
verse.note: The adjective means complete or full-grown, not morally flawless, and is set against the “infants” of verse 14. The noun is singular and is the word for an adult male: the whole community is pictured growing up together into one mature figure. Many modern translations paraphrase as “mature manhood” or “maturity.”

verse.text: so that we may no longer be infants, tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, through the trickery of people, through cunning that serves the scheming of error.
Instead, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ,
from whom the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting joint, as each single part works in its measure, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
So this I say and insist on in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their minds.
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses two words where Greek has one. The readers were themselves non-Jews by birth (2:11), so the term here marks a way of life they have left and not their ancestry.

verse.text: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts.
Having lost all feeling, they have given themselves over to debauchery, for the practice of every kind of impurity, with greed.
But that is not how you learned Christ,
if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, just as truth is in Jesus,
to put off the old self that belongs to your former way of life and is being corrupted by the desires that come from deceit,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “the old human being,” set against “the new human being” of verse 24; the image is of taking off one garment and putting on another. Older translations have “the old man,” and “self” is the common modern rendering. Some interpreters hear a wider sense, an old humanity and the new humanity created in Christ (compare 2:15).

verse.text: to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
and to put on the new self, created in the likeness of God in the righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.
Therefore, having put off falsehood, each of you speak truth with your neighbor, because we are members of one another.
Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,

note.term: Be angry and do not sin
note.traditional: Be ye angry, and sin not

verse.note: The words reproduce Psalm 4:4 (4:5 in the Septuagint) without any introductory formula. The command “be angry” is usually understood as a concession, “if you are angry, do not sin,” and not as an instruction to be angry; some take it as permitting or even requiring anger at wrongdoing. The rendering keeps the form of the Greek.

verse.text: and do not give room to the devil.
Let the one who steals steal no longer; rather let him toil, doing what is good with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with the one in need.
Let no rotten word come out of your mouths, but only what is good for building up as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear.
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, with whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be removed from you, along with all malice.
Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving each other just as God in Christ also forgave you.
So be imitators of God, as beloved children,
and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma.
But sexual immorality and impurity of any kind, or greed, must not even be named among you, as is proper for holy ones,
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people”.

verse.text: nor obscenity, nor foolish talk or coarse joking, which are out of place, but rather thanksgiving.
For you know this for certain: no one who is sexually immoral or impure or greedy—which is to be an idolater—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience.
So do not become their partners;
for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—
for the fruit of the light is found in all goodness and righteousness and truth—
verse.note: Some manuscripts read “the fruit of the Spirit”, which is what the King James Version translates. The earliest and best witnesses read “light”, and “Spirit” is generally explained as a copyist’s assimilation to Galatians 5:22.

verse.text: testing what is pleasing to the Lord,
and take no part in the fruitless works of darkness, but instead expose them,
for it is shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret.
But all things, when exposed by the light, become visible,
verse.note: “By the light” could go either with “exposed” or with “become visible”, and the verb could be passive (“is made visible”) or middle (“becomes visible”). The argument of verses 13–14 is compressed and its exact logic is disputed. The likely point is that what the light exposes is brought into the light and so, like the readers themselves in verse 8, can become light.

verse.text: for everything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says: “Wake up, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
verse.note: The introduction is the formula used for quoting Scripture (as in 4:8), but the lines that follow do not match any known passage of the Old Testament. Most scholars think they come from an early Christian hymn, perhaps one used at baptism, possibly echoing Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1. The source is uncertain.

verse.text: So watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise people but as wise,
making the most of the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.
And do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless living, but be filled by the Spirit,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “be filled in spirit”. The traditional “filled with the Spirit” treats the Spirit as what fills the believer, as wine fills the drunkard. Greek normally expresses that with a different construction, so many grammarians take the phrase as the means or sphere, “by the Spirit” or “in the Spirit”. A few read it as “in your spirit”.

verse.text: speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making music to the Lord with your heart,
always giving thanks for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.
verse.note: Most modern versions soften this to “reverence for Christ”. The Greek word is the ordinary one for fear, used here as in the Septuagint’s “fear of the Lord” for awe before one to whom account is owed. The matching verb closes the section in verse 33, where it is rendered “respect”.

verse.text: Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord,
verse.note: The earliest form of the text has no verb in this verse: it reads “wives, to your own husbands as to the Lord”, borrowing “submitting” from verse 21. Many manuscripts supply a form of the verb, in varying positions. The verb is supplied here so the sentence stands in English, but the instruction to wives is grammatically an instance of the mutual submission of verse 21.

verse.text: because a husband is head of his wife as Christ also is head of the assembly—he himself the Savior of the body.
verse.note: The meaning of “head” as a metaphor is disputed. The majority view is that it implies authority or leadership, which fits the talk of submission here and the use in 1:22. Others argue for “source” or “the prominent one”, noting that this passage develops the image as care and self-giving, not command. The literal word is kept so the head-and-body imagery remains visible.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city’s civic assembly, and in the Septuagint Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. Here the word refers to the whole community of believers, pictured as Christ’s bride and body.

verse.text: But as the assembly submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
so that he might make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word,
verse.note: The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy”, the same word used of the assembly in verse 27. “Make holy” keeps that link visible. Most traditional versions use “sanctify”; the meaning is not in dispute.

note.term: the washing of water with the word
note.traditional: the washing of water by the word

verse.note: The washing probably alludes both to a bride’s bath before her wedding and to baptism. “The word” is literally “in a spoken word”, and what it refers to is uncertain: the proclaimed gospel, a confession or formula spoken at baptism, or Christ’s own pledge to his bride. It is also unclear whether the phrase goes with “cleansing” or with “make her holy”.

verse.text: so that he himself might present the assembly to himself in splendor, without stain or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but holy and without blemish.
In the same way husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself,
for no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the assembly,
because we are members of his body.

note.traditional: members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones”, echoing Genesis 2:23, and the King James Version includes the words. The earliest witnesses lack them, and most editors regard them as an addition. A minority argue they were accidentally omitted.

text.q: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”

verse.text: This hidden meaning is great—but I am speaking about Christ and the assembly.
verse.note: The Greek word means a secret, especially one that God discloses, and English “mystery” wrongly suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Here it most likely refers to the deeper significance of the “one flesh” saying just quoted, which the writer applies to Christ and the assembly. Most versions keep “mystery”. Some interpreters take the secret to be the union of Christ and the assembly itself, or human marriage.

verse.text: Still, each one of you also must love his own wife as himself, and the wife is to respect her husband.
verse.note: The verb is literally “fear”, matching “the fear of Christ” in verse 21 and framing the section. In household contexts it denotes deference and regard, not being afraid, and “fear her husband” would mislead a modern reader. Some interpreters prefer to keep “fear” in both verses to show the link.

verse.text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is the one this translation normally renders “righteous” or “just.” Here it is a neuter predicate meaning “the right thing to do,” and “this is righteous” would be unnatural English, so the traditional “right” is kept.
Some important early manuscripts lack “in the Lord.” Most editors, including the SBLGNT, regard the words as original, and they are translated here.

verse.text: “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise,

text.q: “so that it may go well with you and you may live long on the earth.”

verse.note: The quotation is the commandment from Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16, where the promise concerns “the land” God is giving Israel. The Greek word means both “land” and “earth,” and the letter leaves out the clause about God’s gift of the land, so most translators take the promise here in the wider sense. “In the land” remains possible.

verse.text: And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.
Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in sincerity of heart, as you would Christ,
verse.note: The Greek word for a slave’s “master” is the same word translated “Lord” when used of Christ, and the passage plays on this throughout. Verse 9 makes the point explicit by telling masters that they themselves have a Master in the heavens. “Earthly” renders a phrase that is literally “according to the flesh,” marking these masters as human ones only.

verse.text: not only while being watched, as people-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ doing the will of God, wholeheartedly
verse.note: The Greek phrase is literally “from the soul,” an idiom for doing something with one’s whole self. It can be attached either to “doing the will of God” or to “serving” in the next verse. The Greek edition translated here punctuates it with what follows, and the English is arranged to match, but many translations take it with what precedes.

verse.text: and with goodwill serving as slaves, as to the Lord and not to people,
knowing that each person, whatever good they do, will receive this back from the Lord, whether slave or free.
And masters, do the same to them, giving up threats, knowing that the Master of both them and you is in the heavens, and there is no favoritism with him.
verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to “heaven.” This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it.

verse.text: Finally, be made strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.
Put on the full armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil,

because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verse.note: “Rulers” and “authorities” were ordinary words for human officials, but here, as elsewhere in this letter, they name unseen spiritual powers. The explicit contrast with “flesh and blood” makes this clear. “World-rulers” translates a rare word used in the period of cosmic powers, including the planets thought to govern human fate.

verse.text: For this reason take up the full armor of God, so that you may be able to withstand on the evil day and, having done everything, to stand.
Stand, then, having belted your waist with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
and having shod your feet with the readiness of the good news of peace,
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, and it is translated that way here. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

note.term: the readiness of the good news of peace
note.traditional: the preparation of the gospel of peace

verse.note: The phrase can mean a readiness to announce the good news of peace, or a readiness (some say a firm footing) that the good news of peace gives the one who wears it. The Greek does not decide between these, and the translation leaves the relationship open as the Greek does.

verse.text: in all circumstances taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
with every prayer and petition, praying at all times in the Spirit, and to this end staying alert with all perseverance and petition for all the holy ones,
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

verse.text: and for me, that words may be given to me when I open my mouth, to make known with boldness the secret of the good news,
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas the point here is that the secret is being made known. Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established term, explained as a truth once hidden and now revealed.

verse.text: for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that in proclaiming it I may speak boldly, as I must speak.
So that you also may know how things are with me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make everything known to you.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are and he may encourage your hearts.
Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love.
verse.note: The closing words are literally “in imperishability,” and what they attach to is disputed. They may describe the love of those who love Christ, as translated here and in most modern versions. They may instead go with “grace,” giving “grace and immortality be with all,” or describe Christ as the one who lives in immortality.
